data.title: Beijing to bar young âred-chipâ firms from listing outside mainland China: sources
data.description:
CHINA’S securities watchdog has told some law firms it will not approve plans by red-chip firms to list outside mainland China, people familiar with the matter said, a move that tightens its control of capital raised offshore and could dent Hong Kong’s IPO market.

Red-chip companies are registered abroad, mainly in tax havens, but control assets and businesses in China via equity ownership or contractual agreements.

The structure is favoured by Chinese startups, particularly tech firms, keen to raise capital in places like Hong Kong or New York to take advantage of more relaxed rules and deeper pools of funds available from foreign investors.

The China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) has told law firm representatives in recent days that red-chip companies established after the introduction of new offshore listing rules in 2023 must be re-domiciled in China before they can list offshore, said the people.

The people declined to be identified as the regulatory guidance was confidential. The move is being reported for the first time by Reuters.

China and the US are competing fiercely to gain the upper hand in tech, particularly in AI and semiconductors, which has led to efforts by Chinese authorities to sharpen their scrutiny of technology, data and capital going outside its borders.

The CSRC did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Oversight of red-chip firms has gradually become stricter.

Prior to March 2023, Chinese companies employing overseas holding structures to raise capital abroad did not need regulatory approval. That changed with the advent of the new rules.

Then this year, the CSRC told Reuters in March that it was examining the “necessity and compliance” of red-chip structures, particularly those formed after March 2023.

Despite that warning, some red-chip IPO hopefuls and their advisors have been seeking approval to list outside the mainland without dismantling their existing structure and shifting their domicile back to China, one of the people said.

Most of those applicants failed to convince the regulator that a red-chip structure was necessary, prompting the tougher stance, the person added.

Hong Kong IPO market could be hurt

A drop-off in listings from red-chip firms is likely to hurt but not hobble Hong Kong, the top IPO destination for Chinese firms, which has seen business boom for the past 18 months.

Funds raised via IPOs in Hong Kong during the first 10 months of this year surged 84 per cent from the same period last year to hit HK$404 billion (US$52 billion), though the CSRC has slowed approvals of IPOs since September.

In addition to going slow on approvals for listings by AI, chip and humanoid robot firms after a market frenzy in those sectors, it has more broadly increased its scrutiny as markets have weakened.

Last year, one-fifth of 131 Hong Kong listings approved by the CSRC involved offshore holdings, the majority of which used a red-chip structure, according to Chinese law firm Han Kun.

So far this year, the CSRC has approved Hong Kong listings for just 6 red-chip companies, a sharp decline from 50 approved last year, according to data compiled by law firms and Reuters.

There were nearly 600 listing applications pending in Hong Kong at the end of October, official data showed.

Most of them are mainland Chinese firms though it was not clear how many are red chips given that the number includes applications that were filed confidentially.

There are, however, at least four active Hong Kong IPO applicants which have an offshore holding company structure for their mainland China businesses, according to a Reuters review of filings with the Hong Kong stock exchange.

Any red-chip firms seeking to list in Hong Kong or New York could now face a long wait before coming to market due to the time and costs involved in becoming incorporated in China.

But some, like Chinese AI firm StepFun, have been working on shifting their domicile back to China to pave the way for a planned overseas listing, sources have said. StepFun did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Asked about news of the ban on red-chip firms listing outside mainland China, the Hong Kong bourse said it “welcomes issuers with a range of ownership structures, provided they meet all applicable regulatory requirements in Hong Kong and other relevant jurisdictions.” REUTERS

data.title: Stoneweg Europe Stapled Trust acquires Italian logistics facility for US$66.9 million
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Stoneweg Europe Stapled Trust (Sert) has acquired a fully leased logistics facility in Verona, Italy, for a consideration of 61 million euros (US$66.9 million). This is around a 7 per cent discount compared to its independent valuation of 65.7 million euros as at Sep 22, its manager said on Monday (Nov 23).

It said it expects the facility to be dividend per share and net property income accretive.

The newly completed freehold logistics facility, Verona Freight Village, is located within one of Italy’s premier logistics hubs and ranked second in Europe, based on a 2025 survey, the manager said.

“Comprising approximately 43,500 square metres of lettable area, the asset was delivered to its tenant, Stora Enso, in October 2026,” it said, adding that the asset is fully leased to the global provider of renewable solutions in packaging, biomaterials and sustainable construction.

This is on a 15-year lease, with a mutual break option after year nine and annual rental indexation linked to 100 per cent of the Italian consumer price index.

The lease generates a net initial yield of about 6 per cent, the manager said, above current prime Italian logistics yields of 5.3 to 5.5 per cent with 100 per cent occupancy, “and provides long-term visibility over income and cash flows”.

It also noted the facility’s integrated rail infrastructure, citing the valuation report by Savills that said its direct rail connectivity and Interporto Quadrante Europa location – which provides access to key domestic and international distribution routes – “differentiates it from conventional logistics facilities in the wider Verona market”.

“Savills further notes that the limited availability of comparable rail-served logistics accommodation in the area contributes to the asset’s attractive competitive positioning and long-term income resilience,” the manager continued.

Following the acquisition, Sert’s exposure to logistics, light industrial and data-centre assets will increase from 62.8 per cent to 63.8 per cent. Italy’s share of the portfolio increases from 16.8 per cent to 19 per cent, and Western Europe and the Nordics will account for 90.8 per cent.

Simon Garing, CEO of the manager, called the acquisition another important step in the execution of its strategy.

“We are actively recycling capital into logistics and light industrial assets to increase Sert’s exposure to the sector where we see the strongest combination of income visibility, structural demand drivers and long-term earnings growth potential,” he said.

“The transaction demonstrates our ability to redeploy capital into high-conviction opportunities that are immediately earnings accretive while advancing our target of achieving close to 80 per cent exposure to the logistics, light industrial and data centre sectors by 2028.”

The acquisition, including the purchase consideration, transaction costs and value-added tax (VAT), is funded initially by Sert’s revolving credit facility.

“The manager intends to refinance and optimise the acquisition financing over time through a combination of capital-recycling initiatives, the recovery of the Italian VAT within one year, balance sheet management measures and other financing sources, as appropriate,” it said.

The total purchase cost of the acquisition of Verona Freight Village is estimated to be around 63.1 million euros, excluding the recoverable VAT, but including the purchase consideration, acquisition fee payable to the manager, Italian registration taxes, and other professional and other fees and costs.

The counter closed at S$2.04, down 1.9 per cent or S$0.04, on Friday.

data.title: Stocks to watch: UOB, Hongkong Land, Stoneweg, Marco Polo Marine
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Monday (Nov 23):

UOB : The bank and the municipal government of Guangzhou in China signed a memorandum of understanding on Friday to establish a new technology innovation centre. The proposed centre in Guangzhou will add engineering capacity and specialist expertise to UOB’s technology capabilities. This is UOB’s third technology innovation centre, following its first two in Singapore and Malaysia. The counter ended 2 per cent, or S$0.72, lower at S$35.42 before the news.

Hongkong Land : The property developer has raised its full-year profit guidance, as growth in its Hong Kong and mainland China portfolios led to a 38 per cent rise in underlying profit for its third quarter ended Sep 30. The group said on Friday that it expects a “mid-teens” percentage rise in FY2026 underlying profit, compared with its previous expectation for a result “broadly in line” with the 11 per cent rise in underlying profit in the first half of this year. It also expects growth in its full-year earnings per share “to reach the high-teens”, thanks to its share buyback programme. The stock ended 0.4 per cent, or US$0.03, lower at US$8.39 before the announcement.

Stoneweg Europe Stapled Trust : The trust has acquired a fully leased logistics facility in Verona, Italy for 61 million euros (US$66.9 million). This is compared to its independent valuation of 65.7 million euros, its manager said on Monday. The counter closed at S$2.04, down S$0.04 or 1.9 per cent, on Friday, before the announcement.

Marco Polo Marine : The marine logistics group issued a profit guidance last Friday, saying it expects to report a lower net profit after tax for the financial year ended Sep 30 compared with the previous year. This is mainly due to the absence of a one-off gain from the disposal of the group’s interest in a joint venture recognised in FY2025, and a “significantly lower reversal” of impairment losses on certain vessels in FY2026. The stock finished 5 per cent, or half a cent, lower at 9.5 cents before the news.

data.title: Trump-Xi-Putin summit marks the start of the post-Western order
data.description:
AMERICAN presidents who lose a midterm election have a habit of boarding Air Force One soon afterwards.

In November 2014, a week after the Democrats lost the Senate, Barack Obama flew to Beijing for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit.

Obama returned with a landmark climate agreement with Chinese President Xi Jinping, longer visas for students and business travellers, a deal to scrap tariffs on high-tech products and new military confidence-building measures.

Twenty years earlier, after the Republican landslide of 1994, Bill Clinton went to Bogor, Indonesia, where Apec leaders committed to free and open trade across the Pacific.

Neither trip rescued their fortunes at home. But Americans got something out of them.

Donald Trump, whose party lost both chambers of Congress on Nov 3, followed the script and flew to Shenzhen. If he brought anything for Americans, it is much harder to find.

Symbolism over substance

What the world will remember from the Nov 19 trilateral summit is a photograph.

At Kylin Villa, Xi sat at the centre of the table, with the presidents of the United States and Russia on either side.

Chinese diplomacy has always understood that power is also a matter of staging, and this was a masterpiece of the genre: China as the Middle Kingdom, convening and steadying the world.

The country that built the post-1945 order sat on one flank, at the same level as Russia, an economy of roughly US$2.9 trillion – against America’s US$32.6 trillion – with a declining population and a war in Ukraine approaching its fifth year with no end in sight.

If historians need one image to mark the start of the post-Western order, Shenzhen has supplied it.

Trump rated the summit “12 out of 10”. Analysts around the world are less generous.

Their near-unanimous verdict is that the meeting was heavy on symbolism and light on substance. I can only agree.

An ironic peace declaration

Trump, Xi and Vladmir Putin talked for about 90 minutes. No breakthroughs on Ukraine or Iran. No mention of Taiwan. There was no movement on the rare earth metals Beijing continues to ration, and no arms control was discussed.

The meeting produced a “Declaration toward Peace” that looks as if the surrealist painter Salvador Dali had composed it on an off day: United Nations reform, oil barrels, immunity of heads of state, and nuclear risks.

Tommy Koh, diplomat and Singapore’s former permanent representative to the UN, has called the declaration “absurd”.

It is curious that UN reform has suddenly become a shared priority for three veto powers that have spent decades blocking any change to the Security Council.

Are the three powers signalling an agreement on who should succeed Antonio Guterres, whose term ends in December, as next UN secretary-general?

The second point, a pledge to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products “for the benefit of all nations”, is presented as energy security.

In practice it is a gift to the Kremlin, whose war economy depends on hydrocarbon revenues that have fallen sharply in 2026.

The most troubling is the third point.

The three leaders declared that state consent and respect for the immunities of state officials are “of paramount importance” and that the International Criminal Court and similar bodies “must not abuse their jurisdiction”.

The language serves Putin perfectly: the court issued a warrant for his arrest in 2023 over the unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children. A declaration about peace has turned into a declaration about impunity.

Only the fourth point deserves its place under the title.

The three presidents reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought, the formula Reagan and Gorbachev adopted in 1985, and promised a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation.

The wording is careful. It speaks of “risks” rather than arms control, which China rejects while it expands its arsenal. It focuses on proliferation, the one issue on which those who already have the bomb always agree.

The message for Asia and Asean

Some experts suspect Moscow and Beijing are thinking less about Iran than about Japan and South Korea deciding one day that the American umbrella can no longer be trusted.

That is the real message for Asia. Tokyo and Seoul watched their protector sit in a lakeside villa with their two main strategic adversaries, in a meeting that ran twice as long as Trump’s session with the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi insisted Japan’s interests would not be compromised, while her officials privately questioned Washington’s commitment.

In Seoul, scholars talk openly of the pillars of national security policy being shaken.

After 70 years of loyalty, America’s closest Asian allies may conclude that they have been thrown under the bus, and that the bus is Chinese.

For South-east Asia, and for Singapore in particular, Shenzhen is a warning more than a shock.

This region has prospered in a world where rules, however imperfect, constrained the strong.

A concert of three powers that dismisses international courts and treats the UN as a matter to settle among themselves is the opposite of what middle powers and small states need.

At the Apec table, Singapore’s Prime Minister Lawrence Wong urged the region to keep cooperating even when it cannot agree on everything, and to resist splitting into rival blocs. That is the right instinct.

With Singapore chairing Asean next year, the task is to give real substance to coalitions of middle powers and to keep Asean at the centre of regional diplomacy, so that South-east Asia stays in the room rather than on the menu.

Obama came home from Beijing with a climate deal.

Clinton came home from Bogor with a trade vision.

Trump came home from Shenzhen with a photograph, and the photograph belongs to Xi.

The writer is vice-dean (executive education) and associate professor in practice at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, National University of Singapore

data.title: Trump to welcome investors at gala for his plunging meme coin
data.description:
[NEW YORK] US President Donald Trump will headline his third meme coin gala on Sunday night at his country club outside Washington, DC, for top holders of the tokens, which were once worth about US$75 each but are now valued at less than US$1.

Less than 20 months after the first $TRUMP token gala set off a frenzy among 220 wealthy crypto holders vying for spots at the dinner with the president, interest has waned for the latest affair at the Trump National club in Sterling, Virginia.

Organizers indicated that 185 crypto wallets qualified for the dinner, although the leaderboard on the $TRUMP coin club website listed just 130 wallets when the contest concluded on Nov 16.

Together, those listed wallets only held US$8.6 million — a shadow of the US$148 million listed for the first dinner in May 2025, when a time-weighted holding of US$18.5 million grabbed the top seat.

According to the contest’s website, the top 29 winners — which had the highest time-weighted holdings during the contest scoring period from Sep 30 to Nov 16 — will join a VIP reception with the president and receive a gift bag with Trump swag. The top four also get an 18-karat gold Trump-branded watch.

Trump and his family have monetised his brand through an array of equities and crypto ventures during his foray into politics.

More than half of the digital wallets publicly listed on the contest leaderboard for Sunday’s dinner are tied directly to crypto exchanges that bar US-based users, indicating they are linked to foreign nationals, according to an analysis of blockchain data prepared for Reuters by the nonpartisan, nonprofit consumer advocacy group Public Citizen.

Democratic leaders in the House and the Senate, where the party won a resounding victory in the midterm elections, have vowed to investigate what they say are unprecedented conflicts of interest posed by the Trump family’s business dealings during Trump’s presidency. They also say they plan to push for legislation that would ban such activities.

The Trump Meme Coin project and the White House did not respond to requests for comment, although the Trump administration has long said the president’s business interests are clean.

“Neither the President nor his family has ever engaged — or will ever engage — in conflicts of interest,” White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told Reuters earlier this year. “President Trump proudly made the United States the crypto capital of the world through executive actions.”

The Trump family’s other crypto-connected equities and ventures have also fallen in value to record lows. Together, outside investors in their five main crypto and crypto-linked projects have lost more than US$5 billion, according to a Reuters analysis.

The Trump meme coin has earned the Trump family at least US$635 million, according to the president’s June financial disclosure statement. In total, the Trumps had earned at least US$2.3 billion through April from their four main crypto ventures, including the meme coin.

The president’s stake in a fifth crypto-linked venture, Trump Media & Technology Group, is worth about US$430 million. REUTERS

data.title: Nvidiaâs slump, Anthropicâs listing turn spotlight on Big AIâs need for new governance frameworks
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] When news of Jensen Huang’s extramarital relationship with an Nvidia executive broke earlier this month, it surprised me that many observers seemed to think he had finally crossed the line.

It was already clear by then that Huang had also been having an affair with a woman US authorities believed was a Chinese spy, and that he had misrepresented the nature of that relationship to senior officials at Nvidia for some time.

In my view, this was objectively much worse than an illicit dalliance with a subordinate. The alleged spy was linked to a major buyer of Nvidia chips in Singapore called Megaspeed, which had ties to Chinese companies. This naturally alarmed the US government, and has already led to tighter restrictions on Nvidia.

Last week, the US Commerce Department announced licence requirements for the export of advanced artificial intelligence chips for use in data centres providing remote computing power to China. Licence requirements were also slapped on the export of advanced AI chips to destinations with “unacceptable risk of diversion” – including Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Brazil and Thailand.

These restrictions and the ouster of Huang – who had advocated for China to be allowed access to AI chips, and provided buyers of AI chips with financial support – have felt like a supply shock for the booming technology sector.

Nvidia’s shares sank a further 22.9 per cent last week, despite the company reporting robust third-quarter financial numbers and strong revenue guidance for 2027. Since the end of last month, when the spy scandal began making headlines, Nvidia’s shares have slumped 38.7 per cent.

The S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 have fallen 8.8 per cent and 11.8 per cent, respectively, during the same period.

“Indispensable” CEOs

To be clear, I’m not suggesting that Huang should be excused for his affairs with employees of Nvidia – it later emerged that there was more than one.

Illicit relationships with customers, business partners or subordinates are effectively undisclosed conflicts of interests that have the potential to harm a company and its stakeholders. One might also argue that such lapses reveal character flaws that make CEOs unsuited for their roles.

Certainly, cultural attitudes towards this sort of behaviour seem to have become less forgiving. In recent years, major companies such as Nestle, BP, McDonald’s and Intel have given their CEOs the boot for relationships with subordinates.

Yet, Huang’s involvement with the alleged Chinese spy clearly had the potential to cause far more damage to Nvidia and its stakeholders than his affairs with employees – not least by putting all of them in the crosshairs of the US government.

This case is also perplexing as Huang’s exit from Nvidia appears to have weakened confidence in the company and wider AI ecosystem. Many investors, technology sector luminaries as well as Nvidia’s own employees are now calling for Huang’s return.

Nvidia has said it is not considering inviting Huang back.

The way I see it, market regulators and corporate governance experts should begin thinking hard about how seemingly indispensable corporate leaders such as Huang can be effectively checked; and how to ensure fast-growing companies in important new fields do not betray their stakeholders.

Anthropic’s share classes

Part of the answer may come from the big AI companies themselves. Anthropic, for one, had some interesting things to say during the run-up to its initial public offering.

In a letter to prospective investors, the company’s founders extolled the potential of AI to boost productivity and accelerate the pace of medical breakthroughs, while also warning of the immense harm the technology may inflict on humanity.

“AI has unusually large externalities, both positive and negative. Cultivating the positive externalities, and defending against the negative ones, is to some degree in tension with the natural incentives of a for-profit company, and with the standard governance structure of a publicly traded company,” the founders said.

To address this, Anthropic was formed as a public benefit corporation, which requires its board to weigh the interests of its shareholders against its public benefit mission and the interests of those materially affected by its conduct.

Within that structure, different groups of stakeholders are accorded influence and interest through five different classes of shares.

Most of the control lies with holders of its Class F and Class T shares. The single Class F share, held by an entity controlled by Anthropic’s seven co-founders, has 50.1 per cent voting power.

On the other hand, an independent body called the Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT), holds Anthropic’s single Class T share, giving it the power to appoint four of the seven members of the company’s board.

Anthropic will also issue Class E shares to its non-founder employees over time, giving them a say on some governance matters – including the appointment of one Class T director under certain circumstances.

All the economic benefits of the company belong exclusively to holders of its Class A and Class N shares, though. The difference between the two is that the Class N shares have no voting rights, except where required by law.

The Class N shares are held by Anthropic’s public benefit fund and some strategic partners, such as Amazon and Alphabet. The company plans to contribute 2 per cent of its equity to its public benefit fund for every sustained 50 per cent increase in its share price.

The Class N shares convert to Class A shares when transferred by their holders to non-affiliated parties.

Improve standard practices

Investors who resisted the introduction of dual-class shares in Singapore may well be appalled by Anthropic’s multiple share classes.

Not only will Anthropic’s founders maintain majority voting power even if they dispose of their shares, the trustees of the LTBT may appoint directors opposed to the company maximising its profits. Holders of the Class A shares will also face dilution from the ongoing issue and conversion of Class N shares.

However, Anthropic’s founders pointed out in their letter that the size and structure of the company’s plan to allocate equity to its public benefit fund is “not outside the range” of executive compensation packages at some companies.

It may also be desirable, in my view, for independent bodies of various stripes to have some influence over corporate behemoths that bestride the world.

Anthropic may be more aware of its own power than many other companies in the same league, because of the nature of its business and the fact that it has garnered a US$1.5 trillion valuation within only six years of its founding.

By contrast, Nvidia attained a market capitalisation of US$1 trillion only in 2023, three decades after it began operating. While its CEO Huang should be proud of his achievement, his stunning fall from grace is perhaps a sign that the company needs to be run differently now.

Anthropic’s novel governance framework may well not be the answer, of course – indeed, the company itself says it is a work in progress. Yet, its attempt to improve on standard corporate practices is probably something other companies should emulate as they grow and evolve.

“We will make mistakes, and we expect to learn from others as much as they learn from us. If our competitors adopt our practices and improve on them, we consider that a success,” its founders said.

data.title: COP31: EU rejected climate deal due to backsliding on fossil fuels
data.description:
The European Union couldn’t sign up to a deal at the United Nations climate talks that would have meant the world backsliding on its previous commitment to transition away from fossil fuels, according to its top negotiator.

Wopke Hoekstra, the bloc’s climate chief, told Bloomberg News that the failed COP31 negotiations in Antalya, Turkey, showed that multilateralism is in “dire straits” and that alternatives outside the UN process would be needed to make progress on fighting climate change.

The summit fell short of a major agreement among the nearly 200 nations represented just weeks after the UN warned for the first time that the planet was on course to shoot past its Paris Agreement goal of keeping temperatures from surpassing 1.5 deg C above pre-industrial levels. 

Hoekstra said that a small group of countries were able to sabotage the process to address that problem, a reference to fossil fuel producers.

“The core weakness of the system clearly is that a minority, no matter how small it is, has the capacity to derail the whole process,” Hoekstra said. “This was backtracking on the whole fundament of the world being in overshoot — the basic fact that us burning fossil fuels is at the heart of the planet warming up.”

Hoekstra said that the Turkish hosts of the climate summit were either unable or unwilling to reiterate a landmark commitment made in Dubai three years ago to transition away from using fossil fuels, which represents the biggest contribution to climate change. 

He also called a proposed commitment by the presidency of COP31 to accelerate the use of carbon capture and storage, a controversial technology that some say distracts from the priority of lowering emissions, “deeply worrying.” BLOOMBERG

data.title: Boards need to come clean on directorsâ sustainability vision
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Environmental sustainability is, by now, a well-established concept in corporate governance, with more companies across the Asia-Pacific region reporting that they have made sustainability disclosures and implemented formal board oversight of regulatory compliance.

But whether directors are actually equipped to drive meaningful change in their ESG contributions remains to be seen.

While the international standards being adopted by enterprises set important industry benchmarks for boardroom behaviour, businesses cannot be allowed to turn corporate environmental responsibility into a performative bean-counting exercise.

The Business Times’ newly released Asia Pacific Sustainability Index (APSI) found that 92 per cent of the 700 companies assessed disclosed formal board responsibility for sustainability, while 77 per cent had board oversight of management’s monitoring efforts.

Yet, beyond the issue of how active a role directors in fact play – after all, just 60 per cent of companies reported direct board involvement in determining material ESG factors – is an even more important question: Do they have the vision and skills needed to land an impact?

Many shareholders and external stakeholders simply do not have the information to judge.

Connecting the dots

Perusing annual sustainability reports, observers often find companies reporting their ESG contributions by crunching numbers for metrics such as water and electricity consumption.

To their credit, regional businesses are doing very well on this front.

APSI, which was developed in partnership with the National University of Singapore (NUS) Business School’s Centre for Governance and Sustainability, found that 94 per cent of companies disclosed Scope 1 emissions. Under the widely used Greenhouse Gas Protocol, these are direct emissions from sources the companies own or control. 

Meanwhile, 95 per cent disclosed Scope 2 emissions, or indirect emissions resulting from energy purchases.

Where they fell short, though, was in Scope 3 emissions, which refer to all other indirect emissions caused by business activities. Of the 76 per cent of companies publishing such disclosures, less than one-fifth made reports in more than 10 of the 15 standard categories.

Better information can help organisations “by identifying where emissions hot spots reside in its value chain and potential climate-related risks, particularly transition risks, that may arise”, PwC Singapore’s sustainability and climate change practice leader Fang Eu-Lin told BT.

What’s more, while monitoring enables companies to take stock of their environmental footprint and reduce waste accordingly, tracking emissions data is only the starting point in assessing underperforming areas where companies can improve on sustainability.

Numerous other avenues can be considered, such as rejecting dangerous or pollutive chemicals, or investing in the development of alternative energy sources and materials.

To truly advance sustainability, boards need to have critical judgment and make sound decisions that reflect an understanding of interconnections across sectors and markets.

The quality of sustainability reporting “will improve when companies use the process of creating a sustainability report to evaluate their sustainability targets and progress, and take better measures for sustainability”, Professor Lawrence Loh, director of the Centre for Governance and Sustainability at the NUS Business School, told BT.

Yet, poor visibility on something as basic as their value chains’ emissions suggests that the corporate leaders tackling environmental challenges still lack the ability to see the big picture – and, in turn, the ambition and imagination to come up with credible and viable solutions.

Beyond risks and opportunities

Since business leaders are unable to plan for what they cannot envision, the lingering gap in emissions disclosures could thus be the canary in the coal mine for other shortcomings.

After all, sustainability leadership goes well beyond cuts to direct or even indirect emissions. Though these make for a great start, it is necessary to then plan actionable follow-ups – and many directors may still not have the capacity to deliver this level of strategy and direction.

APSI found that 84 per cent of companies disclosed climate-related risks and opportunities that they had identified, such as the possibilities of floods and droughts.

Yet, just 64 per cent analysed the financial and operational impact of different climate scenarios. Moreover, the vast majority of these were qualitative assessments. Only 28 per cent could produce measurable estimates on how climate change could hit their businesses.

That’s even as quantitative scenario analysis can shed light on how different climate outcomes will affect factors such as operating costs and revenue, as the report’s authors noted.

“Companies could begin by assessing the potential financial implications of physical risks, such as asset damage, operational disruptions and supply chain interruptions arising from extreme weather events, as well as transition risks,” BT’s report suggested.

The estimates generated could allow businesses to “better identify their vulnerabilities, prioritise investments and strengthen long-term strategic planning and resilience”.

The value of detailed scenario planning is obvious – but it requires directors to have the ability to anticipate and analyse complex sustainability-related risks and opportunities.

Unfortunately, they may fall short simply for want of exposure or knowledge.

Only 41 per cent of companies disclosed board members’ sustainability-related competencies, according to the index, while 37 per cent reported recent relevant training.

The paucity in knowledge and training “may result in lost opportunities from tapping sustainability as an economic returns driver”, such as innovating goods and services “that are good for both profits and planet” to gain a business edge, remarked Prof Loh.

Fang added that, while training is important, what’s really key is “whether directors have the skills and practical experience” to properly assess their companies’ readiness and resilience.

Spill the (green) tea

Shareholders deserve to know not just whether directors have the skills needed to offer adequate oversight of corporate sustainability initiatives, but also what is being done to remedy any gaps and help boards continuously build up their expertise and capabilities.

The task of accountability takes on added significance in the light of APSI’s finding that, while 55 per cent of companies said executive remuneration was pegged to sustainability, only 21 per cent specified how performance on these metrics actually translated into compensation.

Added transparency on the link between sustainability outcomes and executives’ short-term and long-term incentives would be to the benefit of stakeholders, the report observed.

Businesses in the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) economies have rightfully been calling for clearer ESG disclosure frameworks and more consistent climate-related standards, as a poll by Singapore’s Apec Business Advisory Council recently found.

But boards must also be prepared to disclose relevant information to their investors in turn.

“A sustainability report is not for the company to feel good about itself,” Prof Loh noted. “It is a report card that tells stakeholders the triumphs and challenges in its sustainability journey.”
